title: Reading the preview before you click
body_md:
## A preview is a peephole, not a permission slip

The button says “View document,” and your thumb is half an inch above it. That label is whatever the sender chose to type. The address behind it is a separate thing, and a preview lets you compare the two before you commit. Think of a peephole in a door: it shows you who is standing outside, not whether they are telling the truth about why they came. Links can redirect, a legitimate hosting service can hold a stranger’s form, and a phone may show only part of the address.

On a computer, hovering over a link usually shows its target in the status bar or a tooltip. Read the whole visible host; a brand name on the left proves little. On an iPhone in Safari, touch and hold a link to open its preview; other apps and phones behave differently. A preview may load part of the page, so for a link you really distrust it can be better to leave the message and get there on your own. If an app hides or cuts off the address, take another route instead of guessing.

### Three things a preview can hide

- **A shortener or tracking link** shows only the middleman’s domain, and the random code after it says nothing about where you will land. Some honest newsletters use them. For an important account action, open the service yourself instead of pasting a sensitive link into a third-party “unshortener.”
- **A redirect** can pass you on after the first address. If you end up at a sign-in or payment form, however you got there, read the address bar at the moment you act. A familiar first stop doesn’t vouch for the last one.
- **Hosted content** lives on a real platform, but anyone with an account may have written it. A genuine forms or document host tells you who runs the platform, not who wrote the form asking for your password or payment. Check the request with the supposed sender through another channel.

Treat the preview as triage. A plainly wrong domain is a reason to stop. A plausible one is only one piece of evidence. And you can often skip the link altogether: if a known app, a bookmark or an official contact route answers the question, the message has nothing more to offer.

### Try it where nothing is at stake

Open a message you already trust and compare a button’s label with the address shown, without tapping it. See whether your device gives you the host, a shortener, or nothing useful. The aim is to learn your own screen, not to test a suspicious link by visiting it.

widget_config.goal: Use a link preview to spot what you do not know, then take a separate route for anything sensitive.
widget_config.today_action: In a message you already trust, look at one link’s address without opening it. Note whether your device shows the full host.
widget_config.scope: A reading habit for everyday links. The interface examples are Safari on iPhone and Gmail on a computer; other apps vary. Every address in the exercises is invented.

sources.title: Gmail Help: avoid and report phishing
sources.scope: Gmail’s hover-over-link check on a computer, and signing in directly instead.

sources.scope: Use contact details you found yourself for any doubtful request.

blocks.title: A shortened payroll notice
blocks.situation: An email says your payslip is ready. The button’s preview shows https://go-payroll.example/r/7Q4 instead of the payroll service you normally use.
blocks.analysis: A short link hides what comes after it. It could be a genuine notification service, but the email cannot prove that. Open your usual payroll portal, or ask payroll through the internal staff directory. Do not paste the link into a public expansion tool.

blocks.title: An ordinary tracking redirect
blocks.situation: A newsletter you signed up for sends you through https://mail-news.example/c/42 to an article on its own site. The label says one thing and the tracking host another.
blocks.analysis: Marketing redirects are everywhere, and this mismatch alone is no sign of fraud. If the article interests you, go to the publisher through a bookmark or a homepage you found yourself. Just never reuse the newsletter’s route for an unexpected request to sign in or pay.

blocks.title: The scholarship form
blocks.setup: An invented exercise. You are a student, and a message about your scholarship application has just arrived. No real form is opened.

steps.prompt: The message says “Application status,” but the preview shows a short link. What can you conclude?

choices.text: The university owns the page it leads to, since the message says so.
choices.consequence: You accept a claim the preview cannot back up.
choices.explanation: A label and a short code do not tell you who owns the final page.

choices.text: The destination is unknown, so check through the university portal instead.
choices.consequence: The link plays no part in your decision.
choices.explanation: The portal can tell you the application status without it.

steps.prompt: You check the portal later, and there is nothing new. A follow-up message says you must pay a processing fee. What next?

choices.text: Contact the admissions office through the directory on the university’s own site.
choices.consequence: The office can tell you what the real procedure is.
choices.explanation: Use contact details you found outside the message.

choices.text: Pay through the message before the deadline runs out.
choices.consequence: You send money on an unverified demand.
choices.explanation: A new request for money needs independent confirmation.

steps.prompt: Later still, the office confirms there is a real application form on an outside hosting platform. What does the host tell you?

choices.text: That the platform itself vouches for every field and payment instruction.
choices.consequence: You trust the hosting instead of the confirmed procedure.
choices.explanation: Anyone can build a form on a platform and use it for any purpose.

choices.text: Only where the page lives. Compare its exact instructions with what the office told you.
choices.consequence: You keep the platform’s identity apart from who wrote the form.
choices.explanation: A real host is no substitute for checking the request.

steps.prompt: The form sends you on to another site before the sign-in. What do you do?

choices.text: Stop and confirm the final address and the expected sign-in method with the office.
choices.consequence: You check the step that matters, when it matters.
choices.explanation: Confirming the first stop does not vouch for the pages after it.

choices.text: Sign in; the first page was confirmed.
choices.consequence: Nobody has checked where the sign-in actually lands.
choices.explanation: A redirect changes who receives your details.

blocks.debrief: The preview showed what you did not know, and the portal and the office filled it in. Go back to any choice where a middle address or a host was treated as proof of the whole request.

questions.prompt: A button reads “Bank statement,” but the preview is a short URL. What do you actually know?

choices.text: Only the shortener’s host. Use your bank’s app to see the statement.
choices.explanation: The code gives no hint of the final destination.

choices.text: The final host is the bank, because the label names it.

questions.prompt: A link opens a genuine document-hosting service and asks for a password. What does the host prove?

choices.text: That the claimed sender approved the document.
choices.explanation: Hosting services carry whatever their users upload.

choices.text: Only that the host is real. Check the request with the sender another way.
choices.explanation: Who wrote it, and what it asks, still need checking.

questions.prompt: On your phone, the preview cuts the host short. What should you do about an account change?

choices.text: Tap through to see the rest, then decide.
choices.explanation: You do not need to follow an untrusted link when you know another way in.

choices.text: Open the service from your saved app or bookmark.
choices.explanation: You reach the task without guessing at a hidden address.

questions.prompt: A newsletter you asked for uses a tracking redirect. Is that automatically phishing?

choices.text: No. Redirects can be legitimate; sensitive actions still get checked separately.
choices.explanation: A mismatch is a clue, not a full diagnosis.

choices.text: Yes. A redirected link is always fraudulent.
